notes:
I read: Enduring Word (David Guzik); Gill, the Pulpit Commentary and the Bible Hub verse pages (which include Ellicott, Benson, Poole, Matthew Henry, JFB, Barnes, Keil & Delitzsch and others); Wesley's Notes; and parts of Precept Austin and StudyLight.

I ran out of search time before reaching the Lutheran, Pentecostal-specific, Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible and Bible Odyssey sites, so those views are missing. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. As far as I got, the traditions don't split along denominational lines. The real disagreements (vv. 4, 6, 12, 14–15) cut across them, and I note them verse by verse.

---

**v. 1: Oppression with no comforter**
- Guzik: this picks up the injustice theme from the end of ch. 3. In an "under the sun" world, where nobody answers for their life in a world to come, the tears of the oppressed are especially bitter and they have no comforter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/
- Benson: no one dared show pity or speak up for them, for fear of being made to suffer in the same way themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-1.htm
- Gill (Baptist): "no comforter" is said twice to stir pity. The oppressor's power is what scares others away from comforting. Gill adds that suffering believers still have a divine Comforter (the Spirit, John 14:16). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: these people as yet knew not the soothing of the Holy Ghost, the Comforter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-1.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): the oppression may come from princes, magistrates, or other potent persons. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Who wrote it (a minority view): the Pulpit Commentary finds it hard to believe a ruler as strong and just as Solomon would just complain about such wrongs instead of stopping them. It suggests the picture comes from later times, perhaps Persian or Ptolemaic rule. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm

**vv. 2–3: Praising the dead and the never-born**
- The usual reading is that this is the "under the sun" view only. Wesley: setting aside the future life, which Solomon doth not meddle with in the present debate. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Precept Austin: The Teacher is not promoting suicide or denying God's goodness. This is in effect a rhetorical lament. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-4-commentary
- Guzik: Solomon could say this only because he had no sure knowledge of the world to come. Jesus said one man would have been better never born (Judas, Matt. 26:24). The despair shows we need an afterlife and a coming judgment. Guzik also sees a hint in "the dead who were already dead" of spiritually dead people who are still alive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/
- Gill disagrees with that last point. He says the dead here are literally dead, "not in a figurative sense". The saying fits only human, earthly judgment, because the righteous dead in Christ really are happier. Gill rejects two other readings: the Jewish idea that v. 3 proves souls exist before birth, and the view that it speaks of the Messiah. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: compares Job 3:11 and Greek poets who said it is best never to be born. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm

**v. 4: Work and envy** (a real interpretive split)
- **Reading A: success attracts envy.** Wesley: All the worthy designs of virtuous men. Envied - Instead of honour, he meets with envy and obloquy. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ Clarke (also Methodist) and Guzik take the same line. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/
- **Reading B: work springs from rivalry** (as the BSB translates). The Pulpit Commentary explains that the Hebrew word can mean either "object of envy" or "envious rivalry". It prefers Reading A as more in keeping with Koheleth's gloomy outlook. It also says "right work" means skill or success, with no reference to moral rectitude. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- Gill gives both readings. He cites the Targum for B (doing good work only to outdo a neighbour) and says it is vanity either way. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- The Expositor's Bible takes B and applies it to modern business competition: the stream cannot rise above its source. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ecclesiastes-4.html

**v. 5: The fool who folds his hands**
- The usual reading is that laziness ruins a person. Wesley: seeing that hard work gets envied, the fool runs into the other extreme. Eateth - Wastes his substance, and brings himself to poverty. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Pulpit Commentary: "eats his own flesh" means he destroys himself. It rejects the view of Ginsburg and Plumptre that the phrase means the idler "still eats his meat". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- Gill: he may also be ruining his family, who are "his own flesh" (Isa. 58:7). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- JFB takes a different view: the "fool" is the wicked oppressor, a self-tormentor never satisfied, his spirit preying on itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-5.htm

**v. 6: One handful with quiet** (who is speaking?)
- **The lazy man's excuse:** Wesley, Aben Ezra (cited by Gill) and the Pulpit Commentary. Wesley: These are the words of the sluggard, making this apology for his idleness. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- **Solomon's own advice to be content:** Guzik reads it as a lesson in contentment (hard work is good, laziness is wrong, but even full hands must learn contentment). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/ Keil & Delitzsch say the "quiet" here has not here the sense of being idle or lazy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-6.htm
- Gill gives both and seems to lean toward the second: a little, held with a good conscience and contentment, is better. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/4.htm

**vv. 7–8: The lonely toiler**
- Guzik: he never stops to ask "For whom do I toil?" Kidner (quoted by Guzik) says this picture checks any excessive praise of hard work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/
- Wesley: he denies himself the comforts God has allowed, which is A dreadful judgment, as well as a great sin. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Gill and the Pulpit Commentary see him as a miser. Gill says some divines call this the worst kind of covetousness. The Pulpit Commentary says greed drives him into isolation, and that applying the verse to Solomon, who had brothers and a son, does not fit. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/4.htm, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm

**v. 9: Two are better than one**
- Wesley: two people living in any kind of fellowship support, encourage, and strengthen one another. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Gill: this ties back to Gen. 2:18 ("not good for man to be alone") and holds in spiritual as well as everyday life. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: compares Christ sending the apostles out two by two (Mark 6:7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm

**v. 10: Lifting a fallen friend**
- Pulpit Commentary: pictures travellers on a rough road, and says the verse may be applied to moral falls as well, such as resisting temptation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- Wesley: "fall" means Into any mistake, or sin, or danger. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/

**v. 11: Keeping warm**
- Pulpit Commentary: Palestine has cold nights, and poor people slept under their outer cloak (Exod. 22:26–27), so a companion's warmth mattered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/4.htm
- Guzik sums up vv. 9–12 as four benefits: getting more done, help in need, comfort, and safety. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/

**v. 12: The threefold cord** (the most debated verse)
- **A plain proverb:** the Pulpit Commentary calls it probably a proverbial saying, like our "Union is strength." https://biblehub.com/ecclesiastes/4-12.htm
- **God as the third strand:** Guzik calls this the common understanding and applies it to marriage. He also suggests Solomon may have meant children. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/ Matthew Henry: Where two are closely joined in holy love and fellowship, Christ will by his Spirit come to them; then there is a threefold cord. https://biblehub.com/par/ecclesiastes/4-12.htm
- A Bible Hub study page says both rabbinic tradition and Christian liturgy apply the verse to husband, wife and God. It goes further and sees a picture of the Trinity, but that is a devotional reading, not an exegetical one. https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_threefold_cord.htm
- Another Bible Hub summary allows either reading: two people plus the Lord, or simply the added strength of community. https://biblehub.com/ecclesiastes/4.htm

**v. 13: The poor wise youth and the foolish old king**
- Pulpit Commentary: Age has only fossilized his self-will and obstinacy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-13.htm
- Precept Austin: Teachability and wisdom are better than power and pride. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-4-commentary
- Who are they? JFB says the youth points to Jeroboam and the old king to Solomon himself. The Pulpit Commentary rejects that and takes it as further proof Solomon did not write the book. The Targum and Midrash read the youth as Abraham and the king as Nimrod. Some Jewish interpreters allegorise them as the good and evil impulses, the new man and the old man (Gill). Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible say no historical identification is convincing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-13.htm

**v. 14: From prison to the throne**
- Benson: the wise youth is often raised up, which was the case with Joseph, Mordecai, and many others. The old king loses his kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-13.htm
- Constable: Ecclesiastes 4:14 evidently describes the poor lad in Ecclesiastes 4:13, rather than the king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/4-15.html
- Precept Austin notes that ancient prisons often held people who couldn't pay their debts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-4-commentary

**v. 15: The "second" youth**
- **The same youth as v. 13:** Barnes says This second youth is generally understood to be identical with the one mentioned in Ecclesiastes 4:13. Pulpit Commentary: It is the old story of worshipping the rising sun. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-15.htm
- **The king's own heir:** Wesley and Benson say "second" may mean the king's son and heir, second in relation to his father. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/ JFB names him as Rehoboam. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Ecc/Ecc_004.cfm
- **The next generation:** Ellicott thinks the Preacher is talking generally about the second generation which shall succeed them. https://biblehub.com/ecclesiastes/4-15.htm
- **"The popular youth":** Whedon translates "second" as ally or companion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ecclesiastes-4.html

**v. 16: Forgotten by later generations**
- Wesley: there are three generations here, and the people will grow as weary of the successor, though a wise and worthy prince, as their parents were of his foolish predecessor. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ecclesiastes/
- Guzik: even a fame that lasts a lifetime is "vanity". Kidner (quoted by Guzik) says he reaches a peak only to be stranded there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-4/
- Matthew Henry contrasts this with Christ's servants, who rejoice in him alone, and they will love Him more and more to all eternity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/4-15.htm
- Precept Austin: only what's done for God truly endures. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-4-commentary
